summary: This cluster centers on a single, thinly corroborated signal: Mihail Eric's account of Stanford's CS146S ('AI-Native Engineering') and the engineering team at Monaco, where the premise is that coding agents can one-shot last year's homework, so the course had to be redesigned around work agents cannot trivially do — learning an unfamiliar open-source repo, proposing a change, and engaging open-source maintainers [14d26da33645360c][537f26930a76d7e3]. Adjacent docs are a broad AI-evals FAQ distilled from teaching 5,000+ engineers and PMs [90580d5369cf9c15], a set of 13 engineering-session notes on evals, context, and systems [0ee42d1cbb1cb2ff], and an unrelated-ish post on model/decision engineering [e6908eaca18c8e77]. For a dev who leads small projects and teaches programming, the actionable read is that the bar for teachable/assignable work shifts toward repo comprehension, judgment, change proposal, and communication rather than one-shot generation — and that eval discipline (as codified in the evals material) is the measurement layer that makes that shift legible. However, the cluster is small, engagement is zero, novelty is very low (0.13), and the core Stanford/Monaco claims rest on a single interview-derived source, so confidence in the specifics is moderate at best.

evidence.claim: When a coding agent can finish last year's homework in one prompt, the course had to change what it assigns — the second run of Stanford CS146S brought open-source maintainers in so students must learn an unfamiliar repo and propose a change.
CS146S is framed around the question 'what happens when students can one-shot last year's homework?' and examines both the course and Monaco's engineering team.
An evals FAQ was curated from common questions received while teaching 5,000+ engineers and PMs AI evals, explicitly flagged as sharp opinions rather than universal truths.
A set of notes distills 13 sessions (~9.5 hours of talks) on evals, context, and systems into about 20 minutes of reading — an example of aggressive compression of engineering learning material.

implications: For a teaching dev: assignments should target repo comprehension and change proposals against unfamiliar codebases, not generation tasks agents already solve [537f26930a76d7e3].
For a leading dev: eval discipline becomes the measurement substrate for both team output and student progress, since 5,000+ practitioners were taught evals as a core skill [90580d5369cf9c15].
Personal productivity/study technique direction: compressing long session material into short written distillations is a demonstrated pattern (~9.5h to ~20min) worth adopting [0ee42d1cbb1cb2ff].
risks: Single-source dependency: the Stanford/Monaco specifics rest on interview-style coverage with two closely related docs [14d26da33645360c][537f26930a76d7e3].
Novelty is very low (0.13) and engagement is zero across all docs, suggesting this adds little beyond known AI-native teaching discourse.
Evals guidance is self-described as sharp opinions, not universal truths — treating it as established practice would be an overreach [90580d5369cf9c15].
Corroboration of 'agents one-shot homework' as a general condition is asserted, not measured, in these docs.

critic.argument: The claim's central empirical assertions — that Stanford's CS146S was redesigned because coding agents one-shot last year's homework, and that its curriculum now centers on repo comprehension and maintainer engagement — rest entirely on one interview-derived source (Mihail Eric's own account, and notably framed around his Monaco work, i.e., a self-promotional vehicle for him and his company). That is a single, interested, non-independent narrator: textbook circularity where the 'corroboration' is just the same person's framing recycled across two chunk IDs [14d26da33645360c][537f26930a76d7e3] that are almost certainly the same document. The adjacent 'supporting' docs (an evals FAQ, 13 session notes, a model/decision-engineering post) do not corroborate the Stanford/Monaco specifics at all — they are topically adjacent but evidentially disconnected, so they inflate the apparent base of support without actually bearing on the load-bearing claim. The only genuinely defensible content is the normative/generalization step ('the bar shifts toward judgment and communication rather than one-shot generation'), but that is a plausible-sounding inference dressed as a finding, supported by low novelty (0.13) and zero engagement — i.e., nobody has independently validated or even reacted to it. No enrollment data, no syllabus citation, no second source, no curriculum artifact. The move from 'one course may have been redesigned' to 'this is how Stanford teaches AI-native engineering' is an overreach from an n=1 anecdote, and the 'eval discipline is the measurement layer' conclusion is an unearned synthesis bolted onto unrelated evals material. This is a lexical/narrative coincidence — 'agents can do the homework, so the homework must change' is a catchy thesis, not a demonstrated institutional finding.
